doc.title: Michael Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 22, 2021

title: Getting in the zone: out-of-body playing, Bird and sports
summary: Preparation, nightly playing, Charles McPherson's Bird story, forgetting what you've learned, and a football analogy.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Is there any preparation that you do before the gig that may assist you in getting to that point where you want to be before you play?

There probably is you know. I haven’t been very methodical about that but I’m sure, you know for example people who meditate regularly have a certain discipline, develop a discipline to put them in a certain frame of mind before they do what they have to do. I could probably count on one hand the times when I reached like what seemed like an optimal state of mind when improvising was almost an out of body experience. I think playing every night, I mean it’s very hard to reach those states of mind when you’re playing a gig, three gigs a month or once a week or something like that. It’s no accident that John Coltrane developed as he did. Well first of all he was a practice-a-holic even when the gig was over he had the horn out. But playing, there’s no experience like playing night after night, five, six nights a week, maybe even playing the same repertoire with the same band on tour, to get you in that place. I was talking about this recently with Charles McPherson just last week, talking about, you know, mind frame for having a, you know, the most desired frame of mind you’re trying to have when you’re trying to improvise. And he said that he saw an interview with Bird where he was, Bird was asked, “So what are you thinking about when you’re playing?” And Bird said, “I look down at my fingers and I can’t believe that it’s me.” Dig it? So that’s what I’m talking about, that out-of-mind — I mean it’s happened a few times where I was playing and I could actually like leave my body and stand over my shoulder and watch what I was doing kind of thing. Sometimes I’ll try and get in that frame of mind while I’m playing — I’ll look somewhere else. I’ll look at the wall. I’ll look across the room. Just as a way to free up my mind, to just be in the zone so to speak.

Do you recall if those rare moments where all that came together were in a trio context or solo piano context? My reason for asking that is I’m wondering, the people that you play with over the years, have you made note of bassists and drummers who are the best helpers for you to enter that comfort zone?
Not particularly. I mean obviously if a drummer is bombastic or a bass player is doing something, if either of them are doing something that’s distracting in some kind of way,

that’s going to be a hindrance. But nothing really more specific than that. I think what I was talking about really happens like during a solo, improvising a solo, where it’s almost like yeah, out-of-body experience where you’re just watching it happen and you’re not standing in the way at all. You know everything is — you’re completely aware of what the chord is of what the tempo is, of all that stuff, but you’re not thinking about it at all. I think Bird was also quoted, there was some interview like about what he practices or whatever, like learn it and then forget it. Not forget it that you can’t do it anymore but forget it that it becomes a subconscious. You’ve mastered it and you don’t have to think about it while you do it, you just do it effortlessly.
It becomes deposited in that part of your subconscious that you were talking about. It can come back for you.

Yeah. I mean there are so many analogies like with sports. People who do things, let’s say collaborative type of engagements where you’re operating on an enormous level of craft and expertise’s but the realization of that business is spontaneous and purely instinctual. You know like when an offensive guard or right tackle is lined up seconds before the play starts, he knows what the play is, he knows what his role is, but what happens within a half a second after the snap is a purely spontaneous event. And that particular player as well as all the players are operating entirely on instinct. So I think there’s a lot of correlation with the improvising jazz musician.
